entries: I wanted you to see what real courage is, instead of getting the idea that courage is a man with a gun in his hand. It’s when you know you’re licked before you begin but you begin anyway and you see it through no matter what.
Harper Lee, To Kill a Mockingbird, ch. 11, to Jem after Mrs Dubose (Atticus Finch) (1960)
Fiction
I should say that courage is a sort of endurance of the soul, if I am to speak of the universal nature which pervades them all.
Plato, Laches, 192b to c (Laches) (trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1892)
Philosophy
Manfully, fearlessly, / The day of trial bear, / For gloriously, victoriously, / Can courage quell despair!
Charlotte Brontë, Life, the closing four lines, Poems by Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell (Aylott and Jones, 1846)
Poetry
It is not in the still calm of life, or the repose of a pacific station, that great characters are formed.
Abigail Adams, letter to John Quincy Adams, 19 January 1780, Adams Family Correspondence, vol. 3, p. 268
Correspondence
Zeus, who guided men to think, / who has laid it down that wisdom / comes alone through suffering.
Aeschylus, Agamemnon, lines 176 to 178, the Hymn to Zeus (the Chorus) (trans. Richmond Lattimore, 1953)
Drama
The virtue of Prosperity is temperance; the virtue of Adversity is fortitude; which in morals is the more heroical virtue.
Francis Bacon, Essays, V, Of Adversity, p. 23 (ed. Mary Augusta Scott, 1908)
Essay

Corrected to the wording of Scott’s edition of 1908, page 23, which capitalises Prosperity and Adversity and prints the sentence whole. The essay first appeared in 1625, where the spelling is Vertue of Prosperitie and Heroicall Vertue, and other modern texts run the clause on from But to speak in a mean.
Although the wind / blows terribly here, / the moonlight also leaks / between the roof planks / of this ruined house.
Izumi Shikibu, Although the wind, the complete tanka, The Ink Dark Moon (trans. Jane Hirshfield with Mariko Aratani, 1990)
Poetry
Life shrinks or expands in proportion to one’s courage.
Anaïs Nin, The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Volume Three: 1939 to 1944, the entry of June 1941, ed. Gunther Stuhlmann (1969)
Diary
He said not: Thou shalt not be tempested, thou shalt not be travailed, thou shalt not be afflicted; but He said: Thou shalt not be overcome.
Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, chapter LXVIII (ed. Grace Warrack, 1901)
Philosophy

Corrected the credit. Warrack’s title page calls the book a version from the manuscript in the British Museum, edited by Grace Warrack, Methuen, 1901, so the source reads ed. rather than trans. The wording is hers and is unchanged. Her introduction prints a variant with distressed; chapter LXVIII, which is the locator, reads afflicted.
There is a stubbornness about me that never can bear to be frightened at the will of others. My courage always rises with every attempt to intimidate me.
Jane Austen, Pride and Prejudice, vol. II, ch. 8 (ch. 31), at Rosings (Elizabeth Bennet) (Egerton, 1813)
Fiction

Corrected to the wording of the 1813 first edition: my courage always rises with every attempt to intimidate me, not at every attempt. Volume II, chapter VIII of that edition is chapter 31 in modern numbering. Elizabeth says it to Darcy at the pianoforte at Rosings.
A joy it will be one day, perhaps, to remember even this.
Virgil, The Aeneid, Book 1, line 203 of the Latin, to his men after the storm (Aeneas) (trans. Robert Fagles, 2006)
Poetry

These are the times that try men’s souls. The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country; but he that stands it now, deserves the love and thanks of man and woman.
Thomas Paine, The American Crisis, Number I, opening sentences (ed. M. D. Conway, The Writings of Thomas Paine, Vol. I, 1894)
Essay
When a man takes an oath, Meg, he’s holding his own self in his own hands.
Robert Bolt, A Man for All Seasons, Act Two, in the Tower, to Meg (Sir Thomas More) (Heinemann, 1960)
Drama
Perhaps all the dragons in our lives are princesses who are only waiting to see us act, just once, with beauty and courage.
Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, Letter Eight, Borgeby gård, 12 August 1904 (trans. Stephen Mitchell, 1984)
Correspondence
To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.
Alfred Tennyson, Ulysses, the closing line, Poems, vol. 2 (Edward Moxon, 1842)
Poetry
So true is it that nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so, and conversely every lot is happy if borne with equanimity.
Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book II, Prose IV (Philosophy) (trans. H. R. James, 1897)
Philosophy

I thought: hope cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist. It is just like roads across the earth. For actually the earth had no roads to begin with, but when many men pass one way, a road is made.
Lu Xun, My Old Home, the closing lines, Selected Stories of Lu Hsun (trans. Yang Xianyi and Gladys Yang, 1960)
Fiction

Corrected: the Yangs print the clause as I thought: hope cannot be said to exist, with hope in lower case. The proposal dropped I thought and capitalised hope, a sentence no edition prints. The words are restored. The volume is Selected Stories of Lu Hsun, Foreign Languages Press, Peking, 1960.
Dance, when you’re broken open. / Dance, if you’ve torn the bandage off. / Dance in the middle of the fighting.
Rumi, The Essential Rumi, ch. 27, The Turn: Dance in Your Blood, p. 281 (trans. Coleman Barks with John Moyne, 1995)
Poetry
Never measure the height of a mountain until you have reached the top. Then you will see how low it was.
Dag Hammarskjöld, Markings, the entries for 1925 to 1930 (trans. Leif Sjöberg and W. H. Auden, 1964)
Diary

Corrected: the entry stands in the opening block of Markings, the entries headed 1925 to 1930, and not in 1958. Hammarskjöld was a young man when he wrote it. The English wording is Sjöberg and Auden’s of 1964 and is unchanged.
Have courage to use your own reason!
Immanuel Kant, An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?, opening paragraph (trans. Lewis White Beck, 1963)
Essay
No coward soul is mine, / No trembler in the world’s storm-troubled sphere: / I see Heaven’s glories shine, / And faith shines equal, arming me from fear.
Emily Brontë, No Coward Soul Is Mine, lines 1 to 4, Wuthering Heights and Agnes Grey, with Literary Remains of Ellis Bell (1850)
Poetry
Corrected: the quatrain is restored to the lineation of the 1850 text, which an earlier rendering ran together as prose. The wording is unchanged and the line heads carry the poem’s own capitals.
Courage is found in unlikely places.
J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, ch. 3, Three is Company (Gildor Inglorion)
Fiction
Oh, I’ve never forgotten for long at a time that living is struggle.
Thornton Wilder, The Skin of Our Teeth, Act III, near the end (Mr Antrobus) (Harper and Brothers, 1942)
Drama
But where danger threatens / That which saves from it also grows.
Friedrich Hölderlin, Patmos, lines 3 to 4, Poems and Fragments (trans. Michael Hamburger, 1966)
Poetry
My own state of mind synthesizes these two feelings and transcends them: my mind is pessimistic, but my will is optimistic.
Antonio Gramsci, Letters from Prison, letter to Carlo, 19 December 1929 (trans. Lynne Lawner, 1973)
Correspondence

Corrected: the wording and the provenance. The proposed English is Raymond Rosenthal’s, not Lawner’s; this sentence is Lawner’s own rendering of the letter. The formula itself is Romain Rolland’s, which Gramsci took up in 1920 and credited to him; here, in prison, he turns it on himself.

It’s really a wonder that I haven’t dropped all my ideals, because they seem so absurd and impossible to carry out. Yet I keep them, because in spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart.
Anne Frank, The Diary of a Young Girl, the entry of 15 July 1944 (trans. B. M. Mooyaart-Doubleday, 1952)
Diary

Corrected: the famous line is not a sentence in this translation but a clause inside one, and the proposal capitalised it as though it stood alone. The wording here is Mooyaart-Doubleday’s, with no comma after everything. The comma and the reading truly good at heart belong to Susan Massotty’s translation of 1995.
Just like moons and like suns, / With the certainty of tides, / Just like hopes springing high, / Still I’ll rise.
Maya Angelou, Still I Rise, lines 9 to 12, And Still I Rise (Random House, 1978)
Poetry
What saves a man is to take a step. Then another step. It is always the same step, but you have to take it.
Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, Wind, Sand and Stars, ch. 2, The Men (Guillaumet) (trans. Lewis Galantière, 1939)
Essay

Corrected: the sentence is in chapter 2, The Men, not in Prisoner of the Sand. Saint-Exupéry prints it in quotation marks as the words of the pilot Guillaumet, who spoke them at Mendoza after walking out of the Andes, so the speaker stands in the source. Galantière’s wording of 1939 is exact.
We know what trembles on the scales, / and what we must steel ourselves to face. / The bravest hour strikes on our clocks: / may courage not abandon us!
Anna Akhmatova, Courage, lines 1 to 4, Poems of Akhmatova (trans. Stanley Kunitz with Max Hayward, 1973)
Poetry
Courage is indispensable because in politics not life but the world is at stake.
Hannah Arendt, Between Past and Future, What Is Freedom?, section II, p. 156 (Viking, 1961)
Essay

Corrected: the section can be pinned after all. The sentence closes section II of What Is Freedom? on p. 156 of the Viking edition of 1961, where it follows the claim that courage frees people from their worry about life for the freedom of the world.
But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea, unchaptered, after the first shark (Santiago) (Scribner, 1952)
Fiction

unused.quote: I rebel—therefore we exist.
unused.source: Albert Camus, The Rebel, ch. 1, the closing sentence (trans. Anthony Bower, 1953)
unused.note: Verified. Held: I rebel, therefore we exist is solidarity in revolt rather than endurance under trial, and the Philosophy lane was full. The quotation carries an em dash that is Bower’s own pointing.

unused.quote: Against the assault of laughter nothing can stand.
unused.source: Mark Twain, The Mysterious Stranger, ch. 10 (Satan) (Harper and Brothers, 1916)
unused.note: Verified. Held: laughter is the weapon here, not endurance, so it wants the lighter month.

unused.quote: Music was my refuge. I could crawl into the spaces between the notes and curl my back to loneliness.
unused.source: Maya Angelou, Singin’ and Swingin’ and Gettin’ Merry Like Christmas, chapter 1, the opening sentences (Random House, 1976)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Maya Angelou stands in July with Still I Rise, and one person may stand once a month.

unused.quote: Do you not see how necessary a World of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?
unused.source: John Keats, letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 14 February to 3 May 1819, the entry of 21 April (ed. Gittings, 1970)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the world of pains that schools an intelligence is a line about becoming, not about holding.

unused.quote: I can’t do much with my hands; so I will make a battering-ram of my head and make a way through this rough-and-tumble world.
unused.source: Louisa May Alcott, Her Life, Letters, and Journals, letter to her father of 29 November 1856, p. 89 (ed. Ednah D. Cheney, 1889)
unused.note: Corrected: this is not a journal entry of 1850. Cheney prints it in chapter five, Authorship, inside a letter written from Boston to her father on 29 November 1856, her twenty-fourth birthday, on page 89 of the Roberts Brothers edition. The tag becomes Correspondence. The wording is exact.

unused.quote: I will not be ‘famous’, ‘great’. I will go on adventuring, changing, opening my mind and my eyes, refusing to be stamped and stereotyped.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, A Writer’s Diary, the entry of 29 October 1933 (ed. Leonard Woolf, Hogarth Press, 1953)
unused.note: Verified. Held for a later month.

unused.quote: I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will; which I now exert to leave you.
unused.source: Charlotte Brontë, Jane Eyre, vol. II, ch. 8 (ch. 23), the orchard at Thornfield (Jane Eyre) (Smith, Elder, 1847)
unused.note: Corrected: the proposal cut the sentence short and closed it with a full stop no edition prints. The 1847 Smith, Elder first edition, volume II, chapter VIII, runs on to which I now exert to leave you, with a semicolon before it. Held: Charlotte Bronte stands in July with Life.

unused.quote: The unknown, the unforetold, the unproven, that is what life is based on. Ignorance is the ground of thought. Unproof is the ground of action.
unused.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, The Left Hand of Darkness, ch. 5, The Domestication of Hunch (Faxe) (1969)
unused.note: Corrected: the novel reads the unproven, not the unprovable. Held: ignorance as the ground of thought is a line about not knowing rather than about courage.

unused.quote: That which does not kill me, makes me stronger.
unused.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Missiles, 8 (trans. Anthony M. Ludovici, 1911)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the most abused sentence in the trade, and at six in the morning it is harder than the month needs.

unused.quote: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
unused.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, Part V, Note to Proposition XLII, the last sentence (trans. R. H. M. Elwes, 1891)
unused.note: Corrected: the translation year. The Ethics sits in Volume II of Elwes’s Chief Works. Catalogues date that volume 1883 in one record and 1884 in another, so the citation now names the revised edition of 1891, George Bell and Sons, whose title page and closing page, p. 271, were read directly.

unused.quote: Nevertheless, not to extinguish our free will, I hold it to be true that Fortune is the arbiter of one-half of our actions, but that she still leaves us to direct the other half, or perhaps a little less.
unused.source: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chapter XXV (trans. W. K. Marriott, 1908)
unused.note: Verified. Held: fortune and the half we still direct is a line about agency, and the Philosophy lane was full.

unused.quote: Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature, but he is a thinking reed.
unused.source: Blaise Pascal, Pensées, Brunschvicg fragment 347 (trans. W. F. Trotter, 1910)
unused.note: Corrected punctuation. The Trotter translation of 1910, printed in the Harvard Classics volume of Pascal, sets a comma after in nature where the proposal set a semicolon. Two separate scans of that printing agree. The semicolon belongs to the later Everyman printing of the same translation, so the year and the wording must match.

unused.quote: If all Men are born free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?
unused.source: Mary Astell, Reflections upon Marriage, Preface to the third edition, London, 1706
unused.note: Corrected to the 1706 third edition, whose added Preface carries the line and prints Slaves with a capital S. Held: the Essay lane was full and the line asks a question rather than answering one.

unused.quote: I do not wish them to have power over men; but over themselves.
unused.source: Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, chapter 4, answering Rousseau on the education of women (1792)
unused.note: Verified. Held: power over themselves is education, not trial.

unused.quote: I do not care what case you put; let them be sea-captains, if you will.
unused.source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, and Kindred Papers, ed. Arthur B. Fuller (1855), p. 174
unused.note: Verified. Held: let them be sea-captains is a line about what women may do, which wants its own month.

unused.quote: But I ask no favors for my sex. I surrender not our claim to equality. All I ask of our brethren is, that they will take their feet from off our necks, and permit us to stand upright on that ground which God designed us to occupy.
unused.source: Sarah Moore Grimké, Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, Letter II, Woman Subject Only to God, p. 10 (Isaac Knapp, 1838)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the Correspondence lane took three and this one belongs with Fuller and Cooper.

unused.quote: The cause of freedom is not the cause of a race or a sect, a party or a class,—it is the cause of human kind, the very birthright of humanity.
unused.source: Anna Julia Cooper, A Voice from the South, Woman Versus the Indian, pp. 120 to 121 (Aldine Printing House, 1892)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the cause of freedom as the birthright of humanity is a line about the common good.

unused.quote: To conquer fear is the beginning of wisdom, in the pursuit of truth as in the endeavour after a worthy manner of life.
unused.source: Bertrand Russell, Unpopular Essays, ch. 7, An Outline of Intellectual Rubbish (George Allen and Unwin, 1950)
unused.note: Corrected: the spelling follows the George Allen and Unwin text, which reads endeavour. Held: to conquer fear is the beginning of wisdom sits close to Kant, and Kant took the day.

unused.quote: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
unused.source: Simone de Beauvoir, The Ethics of Ambiguity, Part II, Personal Freedom and Others (trans. Bernard Frechtman, 1948)
unused.note: Verified. Held: to will oneself free is also to will others free is a freedom line before it is a courage line.

unused.quote: In every town and every village and every mud hut in the world there is always a man who loves children and who will fight to make a good world for them.
unused.source: Lillian Hellman, Watch on the Rhine, Act Three, his farewell to his children (Kurt Müller) (Random House, 1941)
unused.note: Corrected wording: the printed play carries the longer form with the three and joined clauses, not the 1943 film version. Held: the Drama lane took three.

unused.quote: The fairest action of our human life, / Is scorning to revenge an injury: / For who forgives without a further strife, / His adversary’s heart to him doth tie.
unused.source: Elizabeth Cary, The Tragedy of Mariam, the close of Act 4, lines 1 to 4 (Chorus) (1613 quarto)
unused.note: Corrected: the spelling is modernised from the 1613 quarto but the pointing is the quarto pointing, comma in line 1 and colon in line 2. Held: forbearance rather than endurance.

unused.quote: What is there / like fortitude! What sap / went through that little thread / to make the cherry red!
unused.source: Marianne Moore, Nevertheless, the last four lines, in the collection Nevertheless (Macmillan, 1944)
unused.note: Corrected: the quotation now starts at What is there, so the verse keeps Moore own line breaks. Held: the Poetry lane was the fattest in the month.

unused.quote: We never know how high we are / Till we are called to rise; / And then, if we are true to plan, / Our statures touch the skies.
unused.source: Emily Dickinson, ‘We never know how high we are’ (Fr1197, J1176), Poems, Third Series, ed. Mabel Loomis Todd, Life XIV (1896)
unused.note: Corrected: Aspiration is Todd title, not Dickinson, so the poem is cited by first line and standard numbers. Held: Dickinson stands at two for the year and the last slot should be chosen deliberately.

unused.quote: The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.
unused.source: Edna St. Vincent Millay, Renascence, the closing verse paragraph, lines 1 to 4, Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917)
unused.note: Verified. Held: no wider than the heart is wide is a line about the scale of a soul, not about trial.

unused.quote: For I’se still goin’, honey, / I’se still climbin’, / And life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.
unused.source: Langston Hughes, Mother to Son, the closing three lines, The Crisis, December 1922 (the mother)
unused.note: Verified. Held: the Poetry lane was full and Mother to Son wants a month that can give it the whole stair.

unused.quote: Tell me about a complicated man.
unused.source: Homer, The Odyssey, Book 1, line 1 (trans. Emily Wilson, 2017)
unused.note: Verified opening line of Wilson’s Odyssey. Held because January had more openings than days; a line for hard roads.

unused.quote: For there is no friend like a sister / In calm or stormy weather; / To cheer one on the tedious way, / To fetch one if one goes astray, / To lift one if one totters down, / To strengthen whilst one stands.
unused.source: Christina Rossetti, Goblin Market, lines 562 to 567, Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862) (Laura)
unused.note: Verified, the closing lines of the poem. Lifting one who totters is a trial line.

unused.quote: My heart is moved by all I cannot save: / so much has been destroyed / I have to cast my lot with those / who age after age, perversely, / with no extraordinary power, / reconstitute the world.
unused.source: Adrienne Rich, Natural Resources, closing six lines, The Dream of a Common Language (W. W. Norton, 1978)
unused.note: Verified against three postings crediting the 1978 edition; the Norton page itself was not opened. A trial line.

unused.quote: But he that dares not grasp the thorn / Should never crave the rose.
unused.source: Anne Brontë, The Narrow Way (1848), lines 15 to 16, in The Complete Poems of Anne Brontë (ed. Clement Shorter, 1920), p. 145
unused.note: Verified in Shorter’s 1920 Complete Poems, p. 145: he that, not he who. Add the page to the source. Held to keep March under the cap for lines originally in English.

unused.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
unused.source: Li Bai, The Hard Road, closing couplet, The Jade Mountain, p. 70 (trans. Witter Bynner, 1929)
unused.note: Verified. One Bynner poem landed already and only one may stand in a month, and the hard road is a courage line.

unused.quote: Yes, of course it hurts when buds are breaking. Why else would the springtime falter?
unused.source: Karin Boye, Yes, Of Course It Hurts, lines 1 and 2, För trädets skull (1935) (trans. David McDuff, 1994)
unused.note: Verified in McDuff. Held because April landed the other Boye, and one person may stand once a month; the pain of growth suits the month of courage.

unused.quote: The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot for ever fence it out.
unused.source: J. R. R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring, Book I, chapter 3, Three is Company (George Allen and Unwin, 1954) (Gildor Inglorion)
unused.note: Verified with the two-word for ever. Tolkien's small hands is already held for September, so this goes to July.

unused.quote: That’s no way to treat adventures. Never say ‘no’ to adventures. Always say ‘yes’, otherwise you’ll lead a very dull life.
unused.source: Ian Fleming, Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang: The Magical Car, Adventure Number Two (Commander Caractacus Pott) (Jonathan Cape, 1964)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Commander Pott’s counsel is about saying yes to danger, which suits a month of trial.

unused.quote: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
unused.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series, Self-Reliance (James Munroe, 1841)
unused.note: Verified. Held: Trust thyself is self-reliance under pressure more than counsel from an elder.

unused.quote: Living is no laughing matter: / you must live with great seriousness / like a squirrel, for example— / I mean without looking for something beyond and above living, / I mean living must be your whole occupation.
unused.source: Nâzim Hikmet, On Living, Part I, opening lines, in Poems of Nazim Hikmet (trans. Randy Blasing and Mutlu Konuk, 1994)
unused.note: Verified. Held: living with great seriousness is a charge to hold on, which is July.

unused.quote: All letters, methinks, should be free and easy as one’s discourse; not studied as an oration, nor made up of hard words like a charm.
unused.source: Dorothy Osborne, Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple, Letter 33, pp. 160 to 161 (ed. Edward Abbott Parry, 1888)
unused.note: Corrected to Letter 33 in Parry’s edition of 1888, running across pages 160 and 161. The undated heading is kept as Parry prints it.

unused.quote: I wished to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it.
unused.source: Anne Brontë, The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, Preface to the Second Edition, 22 July 1848
unused.note: Verified in the Preface to the second edition of 1848. A plain statement of purpose.

unused.quote: Freedom is always and exclusively freedom for the one who thinks differently.
unused.source: Rosa Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution, ch. 6, The Problem of Dictatorship (trans. Bertram D. Wolfe, 1940)
unused.note: Verified in Wolfe’s translation of 1940. Freedom for the one who thinks differently, a line about dissent.

unused.quote: My way of joking is to tell the truth. It’s the funniest joke in the world.
unused.source: Bernard Shaw, John Bull’s Other Island, Act II, his reply to Nora Reilly (Peter Keegan)
unused.note: Verified as Peter Keegan’s reply to Nora Reilly. Held because the drama lane was already full.

unused.quote: I am large, I contain multitudes.
unused.source: Walt Whitman, Leaves of Grass, ‘Song of Myself’, section 51, 1881 text
unused.note: Verified; parenthetical in the source. Not a beginning line so much as a truth-and-clarity line.

unused.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
unused.source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (trans. Charles Cotton, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877)
unused.note: Verified. Another Montaigne is already held for May, so this goes on to the month of clear seeing.

unused.quote: You can’t get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
unused.source: Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, Book I, chapter 2 (Jake Barnes)
unused.note: Verified, Jake to Robert Cohn. It corrects the traveller rather than sending him out, so it reads as a truth line and not an April line.

unused.quote: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
unused.source: Virginia Woolf, Mrs Dalloway, the opening sentence (1925)
unused.note: Verified opening line. Held: Mrs Dalloway buying the flowers herself is plain speech about a whole life, and it offers no counsel.

unused.quote: There is no foreign land; it is the traveller only that is foreign, and now and again, by a flash of recollection, lights up the contrasts of the earth.
unused.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, The Silverado Squatters, Part II, With the Children of Israel, chapter III, The Return (Chatto and Windus, 1883)
unused.note: Corrected: the sentence is in The Return, Part II. Held: it is the traveller only that is foreign is a correction of the eye, which is June.

report.thinnestLane: the Calendar For Life lane: 6 proposed, 4 survived, the fewest of the four lanes
